questions.q: With type OrderId = string and type PaymentId = string, what does refund(orderId, paymentId) do when the function expects (paymentId: PaymentId, orderId: OrderId)?
questions.explain: A type alias creates a new name, not a new type. Structurally, both parameters are string, so swapped ids compile. A brand adds a member that makes the types different.
options: It compiles: both aliases are just other names for string
It fails at runtime with a TypeError

questions.q: What is a PaymentId declared as string & { readonly [brand]: "PaymentId" } at runtime?
questions.explain: The brand is a phantom: it is erased with the rest of the types. That is why branded ids cost nothing and still work as map keys, in logs and in SQL parameters.
options: An object with a value and a hidden brand symbol
A plain string; the brand property exists only in the type
A string with an extra symbol property attached by the compiler

questions.q: Which assignment compiles, given const id: OrderId = orderId("ORD-7")?
questions.explain: A branded string is a subtype of string, so it fits anywhere a string does. The other direction, and between different brands, is refused. trim() returns a plain string.

questions.q: Where should value as OrderId appear in a codebase?
questions.explain: A cast checks nothing. Confining it to the one function that also validates means every OrderId in the program really passed the check. Any other cast is a hole worth flagging in review.
options: Wherever an order id is needed
Only inside the smart constructor, right after the value has been checked
Nowhere; brands are created automatically by the compiler

questions.q: What does a non-exported declare const brand: unique symbol key give you over a __brand string key?
questions.explain: Nobody outside the module can name the key. The trade-off goes the other way for duplicate package copies: each copy has its own unique symbol, so their brands do not match, while string keys do.
options: The brand is checked at runtime
Other modules cannot read the brand property or write the brand's shape, so it cannot be forged without importing the helper and casting
Compatibility between two installed copies of the same library

questions.q: With @zudojs/constants's Brand (a __brand string key), what is createUserId("USR-7").__brand?
questions.explain: The property exists only in the type, but a string key can be named, so reading it compiles. That mismatch between type and runtime is one reason application code often prefers a unique symbol key.
options: It compiles as "UserId", and is undefined at runtime

questions.q: An app ends up with two copies of a library that brands ids with a unique symbol. What happens when an id made by one copy is passed to the other?
questions.explain: A unique symbol type is unique per declaration. Two declarations, two keys, two incompatible brands. String-key brands avoid this, which is why a framework-wide package such as @zudojs/constants uses one.
options: It works, because both brands are called "OrderId"
It is a compile error: each copy declares its own unique symbol, so the brand types differ

questions.q: What makes a constructor "smart"?
questions.explain: A smart constructor turns "this string passed the check" into a type. Every function that takes the branded type can rely on the check without repeating it.
options: It is the only way to create the branded value, and it checks (and usually normalises) the input before branding it
It caches the values it creates
It is a class with a private constructor

questions.q: Why should parseOrderId trim and upper-case its input before checking it?
questions.explain: If both spellings were accepted as-is, a record stored under one would not be found by the other. Normalising first gives one canonical form per id. createTenantId does the same with NFKC, trim and lower case.
options: To make the regular expression shorter
So two spellings of one id (" ord-7" and "ORD-7") become the same value, and lookups and uniqueness checks cannot miss
Because branded strings must be upper case

questions.q: An order id check uses /ORD-\d+/.test(value). What is wrong with it?
questions.explain: An unanchored pattern tests for a match anywhere inside the string. Anchor both ends and bound the length: /^ORD-\d{1,12}$/.
options: Without ^ and $ it accepts any string that merely contains an order id, such as "ORD-7; DROP TABLE orders"

questions.q: When should a smart constructor return a Result rather than throw?
questions.explain: A user typing a bad id is normal, not a bug, so it belongs in the return type. Inside the program, where a bad id means a bug, a throwing variant (like orderId(raw)) is simpler. Offering both is common.
options: At boundaries where bad input is expected (requests, forms, imports), so the caller can report every problem

questions.q: A function receives an OrderId from parseOrderId. What does the brand guarantee?
questions.explain: A brand records facts checked at creation. Existence and permission can change afterwards and must be checked when the id is used, against the database and the permission system.
options: That the order exists in the database
That the current user may see the order
That the string has the order id format, as checked when it was created
That the order has been paid

questions.q: What is the difference between isPaymentId(value): value is PaymentId and parsePaymentId(raw): Result<PaymentId, string> in the lesson?
questions.explain: A guard cannot change the value, so it cannot turn "pay-88" into "PAY-88". Use guards for values already in canonical form, such as ids read back from your own database.
options: The guard validates; the parser does not
The guard only checks and narrows the existing variable; the parser may also normalise and returns a new value
The guard throws on bad input

questions.q: Why does const total: Kobo = a + b fail when a and b are both Kobo?
questions.explain: Operators and methods return the base type. A helper such as addKobo(a, b) re-brands through the constructor, which also checks that the result is still a safe integer.
options: The + operator returns a plain number; the compiler does not know the sum of two kobo amounts is kobo
Because Kobo is a string at runtime

questions.q: What does TypeScript report for if (paidNaira === expectedKobo) with Naira and Kobo brands?
questions.explain: The two brands have different literal types on the same key, so no value can be both. A comparison between them is always false, and TypeScript flags it: a bug that would otherwise fail silently forever.
options: TS2367: the comparison appears to be unintentional because the types have no overlap
TS2322: the types are not assignable

questions.q: What does createUserId from @zudojs/constants do with the empty string ""?
questions.explain: The id constructors (createUserId, createEventId, createRequestId…) are labelled casts. createTenantId, createEmailAddress, createTimestamp and createUrl validate. Know which kind you call.
options: Returns it, branded as a UserId: this constructor only applies the brand

questions.q: Why does createTenantId reject "acme/../billing"?
questions.explain: Rejecting dangerous characters once, in the constructor, means no use site has to escape them. That is the pay-off of validating on creation.
options: Tenant ids must be shorter than 10 characters
Tenant ids end up in cache keys, schema names and file paths, so anything that could act as a separator or path segment is refused

questions.q: An OrderId is written to the database and read back. What type does it have when it comes back, and what should happen?
questions.explain: Brands are erased, so nothing survives a trip through JSON, a database or a URL. Parse at every boundary where data enters the program.
options: Still OrderId: brands are stored with the value
A plain string (or unknown); the repository must parse it into an OrderId again

questions.q: A project uses both a Zod schema with .brand<"OrderId">() and a hand-written Brand<string, "OrderId">. Are the two OrderId types compatible?
questions.explain: A brand is a property on a particular key. Zod's $brand and your [brand] symbol are different keys, so values from one do not fit the other.
options: No: each library uses its own brand key, so they are different types; pick one source of branded types
Only if the regex is the same

questions.q: Which value gains the most from a brand?
questions.explain: Brand what gets mixed up and costs money or data when it does: ids that travel together, units, validated strings. Local values that never cross a function boundary gain nothing.
options: A loop counter inside one function
An amount of money that some functions take in kobo and others in naira

questions.q: Why do banks often express rates in basis points (7.5% = 750 bp)?
questions.explain: 7.5 could be a percent or a (wrong) fraction; 0.075 could be mistaken for a percent. A whole number of basis points behind a BasisPoints brand leaves no room for either reading.
options: Basis points are more precise than percentages
An integer rate has no "percent or fraction?" ambiguity and no floating-point noise, and a brand makes the unit explicit

questions.q: The lesson's naira constructor allows a tiny difference when checking for two decimals. Why not test Math.round(amount * 100) === amount * 100?
questions.explain: Decimal fractions are not exact in binary. A tolerance of a millionth of a kobo absorbs that noise while still rejecting a real third decimal like ₦50.555, which is half a kobo away from a whole number.
options: Floating-point makes 19.99 * 100 equal 1998.9999999999998, so an exact test would reject an everyday price
It does not work for negative numbers

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The input is normalised before the anchored test, so the spaced lower-case id is accepted in canonical form. ORD- has no digits, ORD-12x has a suffix, and leading zeros are allowed by this pattern.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The unanchored pattern finds ORD-7 inside the sentence and says yes. A smart constructor with that pattern would brand the whole sentence as an order id.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: At runtime a branded string is a plain string, so every string method and template works. The methods return plain strings, which is right: a lower-cased SKU is not a valid SKU.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The brand has no runtime form, so JSON sees an ordinary string, and what comes back is an ordinary string too. It must be parsed into a PaymentId again.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 19.99 is not exactly representable in binary, so the product is a hair below 1999. Rounding gives the right number of kobo, and a tolerance check accepts it; an exact equality check would have refused it.
questions.code:
const amount = 19.99;
console.log(amount * 100, Math.round(amount * 100), Math.abs(amount * 100 - Math.round(amount * 100)) < 1e-6);

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Rounding each share separately loses a kobo. Giving the leftover kobo one at a time to the first shares keeps the total exact, which is how payment systems allocate money.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Branded strings are compared as strings, so they work as Map keys, and a normalising constructor makes different spellings find the same entry.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Math.max returns a plain number (the brand is gone), and adding 7.5% produces a fraction of a kobo. The constructor refuses it instead of silently storing 440,803.75; the fix is to round first, kobo(Math.round(highest * 1.075)), which is what the money helpers do.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: createTenantId normalises (trim, lower case) and rejects the space, so two spellings become one tenant. createUserId validates nothing: it brands even a string of spaces.

questions.q: A smart constructor quotes at most 40 characters of bad input in its error. What does this print?
questions.explain: "TypeError: not a SKU: " is 22 characters, then 40 X's inside two quotes: 22 + 42 = 64. Bounding what you echo keeps a 10,000-character attack string out of your logs.

questions.q: Finish parsePaymentId: trim and upper-case the input, then accept only PAY- followed by 1 to 12 digits. Return a Result. The program should print PAY-88 | not a payment id: "ORD-7" | not a payment id: "PAY-".
questions.explain: The cast happens on exactly one line, right after the anchored test passed. Everything that receives a PaymentId from here on can trust its format.
questions.expected: PAY-88 | not a payment id: "ORD-7" | not a payment id: "PAY-"

questions.q: Finish kobo (accept only safe integers, otherwise throw a RangeError) and addKobo (sum any number of amounts and re-brand). The program should print 2138750 RangeError.
questions.explain: Number.isSafeInteger rejects fractions, NaN, Infinity and integers too large to be exact. addKobo re-brands through kobo, so even the sum is checked.

questions.q: Finish the type guard isOrderId (exact format ORD- plus 1 to 12 digits, no normalising), then keep only the order ids from a mixed list. The program should print ORD-1,ORD-22.
questions.explain: Passing a type guard to filter narrows the result to OrderId[] without a cast. A guard cannot change the value, so the lower-case ord-2 is rejected rather than normalised.

questions.q: Finish formatKobo: format an amount in kobo as naira with thousands separators and two decimals, and a leading minus for negatives. The program should print ₦21,387.50 -₦25.00 ₦0.05.
questions.explain: Taking the parameter as Kobo means the function cannot be handed naira by mistake: the unit is in the signature. The regular expression inserts a comma before every group of three digits that ends the whole part.

questions.q: Finish applyRate(amount, rate): rate is in basis points (750 = 7.5%). Return the result in kobo, rounded to the nearest kobo. The program should print 75000 1339 0.
questions.explain: 10,000 basis points are 100%, so the rate divides by 10,000. 17,850 × 750 / 10,000 = 1,338.75, which rounds to 1,339 kobo; 5 kobo at 7.5% rounds to nothing. Round once, where the calculation ends.

questions.q: Finish parseEmail: trim and lower-case, then accept only a simple local@domain.tld shape. Return undefined for anything else. The program should print true ada@example.com undefined.
questions.explain: Normalising makes the sign-up spelling and the login spelling the same Email, so they reach the same account. The format check is deliberately loose; only a confirmation email proves an address works.

questions.q: Finish parseSkus: normalise each raw SKU (trim, upper case), keep only valid ones (2 to 8 letters, a hyphen, 1 to 4 digits), and remove duplicates while keeping the first-seen order. The program should print RICE-5,OIL-1 | bad: tv, SALT.
questions.explain: Deduplicating after normalising is what makes rice-5 and RICE-5 one product. A Set keeps insertion order, and branded strings compare as strings, so it works directly on Sku values.
